commercialRules.name: Energy & Water Reporting By-law - Toronto Municipal Code Chapter 367, Building Emissions Performance
commercialRules.summary: Adopted Dec 15, 2023 (By-law 1283-2023) and in force since Jan 1, 2024. Owners report annual energy and water data to the City through ENERGY STAR Portfolio Manager, in addition to Ontario's EWRB. The City says buildings over the size threshold must report 'regardless of property use' (unlike EWRB, which exempts some types); exemptions or extensions can be requested in writing. The City publishes building-level data under its disclosure policy. By-law 1487-2025 (enacted Dec 17, 2025, in force Jan 1, 2026) moved the start date for 10,000-49,999 sq ft buildings from 2026 to 2027.
commercialRules.thresholds: Buildings 4,645 m2 (50,000 sq ft) and larger: reporting since 2024. Buildings 929-4,644 m2 (10,000-49,999 sq ft): must begin reporting in 2027. Buildings 9,290 m2 (100,000 sq ft) and larger: certified-professional verification in the first reporting year and every fifth year.
commercialRules.deadline: First business day of July (July 2, 2026 for 2025 data); the provincial EWRB deadline is July 1.

commercialRules.name: Building Emissions Performance Standards (BEPS)

If adopted, BEPS would sit in Chapter 367. Low-rise residential (3 storeys or less) would be exempt from any BEPS proposal.

commercialRules.name: Règlement 21-042 sur la divulgation et la cotation des émissions de GES des grands bâtiments
commercialRules.summary: Adopted Sept 27, 2021. Owners of existing commercial, institutional and residential buildings must disclose the previous year's energy consumption (for GHG calculation) through ENERGY STAR Portfolio Manager, with Hydro-Québec and Énergir data exchange. Buildings whose assessment unit is predominantly industrial (CUBF codes 2/3) are excluded. The by-law provides for an A-F GHG-intensity rating (kg CO2e/m2, absolute scale): BOMA Québec (industry association) reported that Ordonnance no 1 adding the rating methodology came into force Sept 23, 2025, that only the building's address and rating would be published on the City's website, and that posting the rating at building entrances is not in force. The City's zero-emission roadmap (updated Mar 4, 2026) lists, as upcoming measures for buildings of 2,000 m2+, posting an A-F rating at entrances and gradually tighter GHG emission limits reaching zero emissions by 2040 - no dates given. The City's Nov 2023 guide says data may be self-declared and there is 'for now' no obligation to have it verified by a professional (compliance inspections can occur).
commercialRules.thresholds: 2,000 m2 (21,528 sq ft) or larger, or 25+ dwelling units (phased: 15,000 m2+ non-residential and City-owned 2,000 m2+ from 2022; 5,000 m2+ and 50+ units from 2023; 2,000 m2+ and 25+ units from 2024).
commercialRules.deadline: June 30 each year (for the previous calendar year).
commercialRules.note: Rating status comes from an industry source (BOMA Québec, Oct 30, 2025); the City's by-law page does not describe it. The City's current guide (Aug 2026) and the consolidated by-law text could not be opened (Constellio viewer / robots-blocked). Quebec's provincial regulation (rules.provinces.QC) also applies from 2027.

commercialRules.name: Annual Greenhouse Gas and Energy Limits By-law No. 13472
commercialRules.status: in force - enforcement paused since May 21, 2026
commercialRules.summary: Enacted July 20, 2022. Requires annual energy and carbon reports through ENERGY STAR Portfolio Manager, and sets greenhouse gas intensity (GHGI) limits based on natural gas and district energy use for space and water heating (electricity excluded). On May 21, 2026 Council directed staff to pause enforcement; the City says there are no penalties for not reporting, staff will review the by-law and report back in the first half of 2027, and complete reports received by Sept 1 get a comparison scorecard.
commercialRules.thresholds: Reporting: commercial or multi-family residential buildings 4,645 m2 (50,000 sq ft) or larger, phased in by occupancy and size (assembly/business/mercantile/industrial occupancies 9,290 m2+ reported 2023 data by June 1, 2024 and 4,645-9,290 m2 reported 2024 data by June 1, 2025; care and residential occupancies 9,290 m2+ reported 2024 data by June 1, 2025 and 4,645-9,290 m2 reported 2025 data by June 1, 2026). GHGI limits: office (Group D) buildings 9,290 m2+ 25 kg CO2e/m2 and retail (Group E) buildings 9,290 m2+ 14 kg CO2e/m2 from 2026, falling to 0 by 2040; heat energy intensity limit 0.09 GJ/m2 from Jan 1, 2040.
commercialRules.deadline: June 1 each year (by-law); scorecards for reports received by Sept 1.
commercialRules.note: Phasing and limit values are from the by-law PDF as posted (enactment version, no amendments shown). The pause means the requirement still exists but is not enforced pending the 2027 review.

coAlarms.summary: The Ontario Fire Code requires CO alarms in existing homes, not just new builds. The rule came into force 2014-10-15 (O. Reg. 194/14), with compliance required by 2015-04-15 for buildings with six or fewer suites and by 2015-10-15 for larger buildings. At that point alarms were required next to each sleeping area. O. Reg. 87/25 (filed 2025-06-04) replaced Section 2.16 effective 2026-01-01. Alarms are now required next to each sleeping area AND on every storey without a sleeping area. Hardwired, battery or plug-in alarms are all allowed. The homeowner is responsible in an owner-occupied home and the landlord in a rental. The section does not apply to a building whose CO alarms were installed under the Building Code as it read on or after 2025-01-01.

Reg. 278/05 governs contractors: asbestos-containing material means 0.5%+ asbestos by dry weight, and work is classed as Type 1, 2 or 3, each with required procedures and training. An owner must have materials examined and a report prepared before tendering or arranging demolition, alteration or repair, but that duty does not apply to an owner of a private residence occupied by the owner or their family, or to an owner-occupied residential building of four units or fewer.
keyPoints: O. Reg. 278/05 s. 10: owner examination and report before requesting tenders or arranging demolition, alteration or repair.
O. Reg. 278/05 s. 2(4): exempts an owner of a private residence occupied by the owner or family, and an owner-occupied residential building of 4 or fewer units.
O. Reg. 278/05 s. 11: advance notice required for Type 3 operations and certain Type 2 operations. Consolidated to 2026-07-01; O. Reg. 115/26 only updated respirator certifications.
OHSA s. 3(1): the Act does not apply to work done by the owner or occupant in or about a private residence.
OHSA s. 30: before beginning a project, the owner must determine which designated substances are present and give the list to bidders and contractors.

Waste: R.R.O. 1990, Reg. 347, s. 17. No person may manage asbestos waste except as prescribed. It may leave the site only for a waste disposal site whose operator has agreed to accept it and been told when it will arrive. It must be in rigid, sealed, impermeable containers (a cardboard box needs a sealed 6-mil polyethylene bag inside), and containers and vehicles must be marked.

wells.summary: Ontario private well owners can have their water tested for bacteria free of charge through Public Health Ontario (PHO) laboratories: pick up a sample kit from a PHO lab, the local public health unit or one of its designated pickup locations, then drop the sample back off (results are available through PHO's online Water Testing Portal). PHO tests only for the indicator bacteria E. coli and total coliforms; chemical testing (e.g., nitrate, sodium, metals) must go to a licensed private laboratory, which charges a fee. The provincial fact sheet only says to test regularly, while local health units (e.g., Ottawa, Durham, York, Halton, Hamilton, Waterloo Region) recommend at least three times a year: spring, summer and fall.
wells.cost: Free for bacterial testing through PHO. Chemical testing at licensed private labs is fee-based (the province does not publish prices). Some health units add extras: Halton Region tests nitrate free; Region of Waterloo charges $21.40 each for nitrate or fluoride tests.
wells.tests: Free PHO test: indicator bacteria only (total coliforms and E. coli). No chemical testing.
wells.frequency: Province: test 'regularly' (no fixed schedule; more testing after spring melt and unusual events). Local health units: at least 3 times a year (spring, summer, fall), plus after flooding, heavy rain or well work.
wells.bottles: Free kits from PHO laboratories, local public health units and their designated pickup locations (regional offices, libraries, municipal offices, some rural stores); Halton also mails bottles on request.
wells.notes: Ontario's Auditor General (2025, reported by CBC) estimated about 1.3 million Ontarians rely on private wells and fewer than one-third had tested in the previous 12 months. A 2023 AG report said PHO had proposed a 'gradual discontinuation' of free private water testing; the Health Minister said in 2024 it would be kept, and PHO was still promoting free testing in June 2026.

Covered types include multi-unit residential (7+ self-contained units), office, retail/services, hospitality, entertainment/recreation, industrial/warehousing, institutional and 'other' (MPAC property codes); exemptions exist. The province publishes building-level intensities, ENERGY STAR scores and GHG intensity (not totals or floor area) on the Ontario Data Catalogue. Toronto buildings must report to both the province and the city.

coAlarms.summary: Quebec has no province-wide CO alarm requirement for existing houses. In those buildings, art. 359 requires a CO alarm in a dwelling unit, seniors' residence or supervised residence that contains a combustion appliance or has direct access to an indoor parking garage. LégisQuébec shows this version of art. 359 in force from 2014-03-18. The RBQ says single-family dwellings fall under municipal regulations, and Québec.ca tells residents to ask their municipal fire service about local CO alarm rules. So whether a house needs an alarm depends on the municipality.

asbestos.summary: CNESST rules require employers to check for the presence and type of asbestos before any work likely to release asbestos dust (RSST s. 69.11; Construction Safety Code s. 3.23.3). Employers must also inspect buildings built before 1990-02-15 for sprayed asbestos (flocages) and before 1999-05-20 for asbestos thermal insulation (calorifuges) (RSST s. 69.3). Québec.ca tells homeowners to have suspect materials checked by a qualified contractor or an IRSST-recognized lab and to never do asbestos work themselves.
keyPoints: The condition of asbestos flocking and insulation must be checked at the initial inspection and every 2 years after that (RSST s. 69.8).
Quebec's regulatory threshold is 0.1% asbestos in a material (RSST art. 62 and section IX.I; CSTC section 3.23). Per the IRSST, this differs from other provinces.

Québec.ca (updated 2021-01-12) says to hire an RBQ-licensed contractor (subcategory 2.7, 7, 1.2 or 1.3) and get a written commitment to follow the Construction Safety Code. It adds that Quebec has no official accreditation or certification program for asbestos professionals.
No asbestos waste or landfill rule was checked for Quebec.

wells.summary: Quebec has no free provincial testing service for private wells: owners send samples to a laboratory accredited by the Environment ministry (list kept by the CEAEQ, which itself does not test water for individuals), and the lab supplies the sample containers and instructions. The ministry recommends a microbiological analysis (E. coli, enterococci, total coliforms) at least twice a year, in spring and fall, and a physico-chemical analysis (arsenic, manganese, barium, nitrates-nitrites, chlorides, sodium, iron, sulfates, fluorides, hardness) at least once while the well is in use, plus nitrates-nitrites every spring and fall in farm areas or where homes have individual septic systems.
wells.cost: Paid by the owner; the CEAEQ lab list states analyses are a paid service priced by each lab. A provincially funded guide (moneaumonpuits.ca) says to expect from a few tens to a few hundred dollars per analysis, depending on the tests.
wells.tests: Microbiological: E. coli, enterococci, total coliforms. Physico-chemical (at least once): arsenic, manganese, barium, nitrates-nitrites, chlorides, sodium, iron, sulfates, fluorides, total hardness.
wells.frequency: Microbiological at least twice a year (spring and fall); physico-chemical at least once during the period the well is used; nitrates-nitrites each spring and fall in agricultural areas or where septic systems are individual.
wells.bottles: From the accredited laboratory you choose (ministry leaflet); moneaumonpuits.ca adds that the municipality may also provide them.

commercialRules.summary: Enacted by Ministerial Order 2026-0013 (June 9, 2026), published in the Gazette officielle du Québec on June 23, 2026 and in force on the 15th day after publication. Owners must declare each building's energy consumption and costs by source and billing period (first declaration: the two previous calendar years; then the previous year) on the ministry's platform by June 30 each year. Declarations must be verified at least once every four years by a member of a listed professional order (e.g., engineers, architects, CPAs, technologists). Energy distributors must provide digital platforms to transfer consumption data; Quebec's page points owners to ENERGY STAR Portfolio Manager with automatic transfer from Hydro-Québec and Énergir. Excludes buildings under construction or with a demolition permit, agricultural buildings, metro facilities, and buildings on sites whose main activity is manufacturing (NAICS 31-33), mining (21) or water/sewer (2213). Administrative penalties $250-$5,000 and fines up to $3,000,000.
commercialRules.thresholds: From Jan 1, 2027: buildings of 5,000 m2+ (not exclusively residential), residential or partly residential buildings with 50+ units, and buildings owned by public bodies other than municipal bodies (buildings under 100 m2 excepted, subject to a metering condition in the text). From Jan 1, 2028: buildings of 2,000 m2+ (not exclusively residential) and residential buildings with 25+ units.
commercialRules.deadline: June 30 each year; first declaration June 30, 2027 (2025 + 2026 data) for the 2027 group; June 30, 2028 for the 2028 group. Buildings acquired less than 90 days before June 30: by September 30.
commercialRules.note: The published regulation covers declaration and verification only; no GHG/energy rating ('cote') requirement appears in its text. The text does not mention Montréal's by-law 21-042, so Montréal buildings may face both obligations (not confirmed).

coAlarms.summary: B.C.'s fire-safety bulletin says: 'While carbon monoxide alarms are not mandatory in B.C., it is recommended that alarms be installed if a home has a fuel-burning appliance, fireplace or attached garage.' For new construction, BC Building Code Article 9.32.4.2 requires CO alarms in buildings with a residential occupancy that are served by or contain a fuel-burning appliance, or contain a storage garage. The 2024 BCBC keeps this requirement and applies to building permits applied for on or after 2024-03-08. Locally, the City of Vancouver's Fire By-law requires CO alarms in every dwelling unit, new or older, that has an attached garage or a fuel-fired appliance, or shares a wall or floor with a parking garage or a service room containing a fuel-fired appliance.

asbestos.summary: Before demolition, salvage or renovation of a building, the employers doing the work and the owner must have a qualified person inspect it, sample it and identify hazardous materials such as asbestos and lead, with a written report kept at the worksite (OHS Regulation s. 20.112). Since 2024-01-01, asbestos abatement contractors must be licensed by WorkSafeBC to operate in B.C., and anyone doing abatement work must complete mandatory training and hold a certificate.
keyPoints: Licensing and certification come from Workers Compensation Act amendments made in spring 2022. WorkSafeBC began accepting licence applications in September 2023 and published its online registry of licensed asbestos abatement contractors on 2023-11-20. B.C. was the first Canadian jurisdiction to license this work.
Identified hazardous materials must be safely contained or removed (s. 20.112(5)).
WorkSafeBC runs a residential demolition/renovation asbestos enforcement initiative that checks, among other things, that the hazardous materials inspection report is on site.
No asbestos waste or landfill rule was checked for B.C.
asbestos.law: Workers Compensation Act (licensing/certification, 2022 amendments); OHS Regulation Part 6 and s. 20.112

wells.summary: We found no free public testing program for private wells in B.C.: HealthLinkBC tells owners to use a qualified laboratory (searchable in the CALA directory), which provides the sample bottles and instructions, and the lab charges for the analysis. HealthLinkBC names nitrates, fluoride and metals such as arsenic, lead, copper and manganese as the most common chemicals of concern in B.C. groundwater.
wells.cost: Fee paid to the private lab; no provincial price published. Some local governments subsidize tests (e.g., the Regional District of Nanaimo rebates 50% of a qualifying test, up to $350).
wells.tests: Bacteria (total coliforms, E. coli); chemistry packages chosen with the lab (nitrate, fluoride, metals such as arsenic, lead, copper, manganese).
wells.frequency: Bacteria at least once a year (and immediately after changes in clarity, colour or taste); chemistry when the well is completed and annually thereafter.
wells.notes: No provincial free-testing program was found; local programs exist in some areas (RDN rebate; Township of Langley Private Well Network lab discount).

asbestos.summary: Alberta's OHS Code (Part 4, chemical hazards) requires employers to minimize asbestos release and to seal and label asbestos waste. Workers entering an asbestos restricted area need government-approved training and a valid asbestos worker certificate. Anyone planning asbestos removal, or demolition or renovation of a building containing asbestos, must notify Alberta OHS at least 72 hours before starting.
keyPoints: Asbestos worker certificates expire 3 years from the date of issue.
Per the Alberta Asbestos Abatement Manual, asbestos-containing material may be left in place during demolition only with an acceptance under OHS Code s. 34.

Waste must go in sealed containers impervious to asbestos and be labelled 'Carcinogenic – Do not inhale dust'. The manual also says the landfill must be informed in writing that the waste contains asbestos.
The manual PDF reviewed is the August 2019 edition (ASB001).
asbestos.law: Occupational Health and Safety Code (Part 4 and related parts); Alberta Asbestos Abatement Manual

wells.summary: Alberta Health Services (AHS) Environmental Public Health tests water from private drinking-water supplies (wells, cisterns, surface water) free of charge: a bacteria test (total coliforms and E. coli) and a chemical and trace-metals test. Bottles are picked up and dropped off at AHS facilities (listed on InformAlberta); AHS will not test samples collected for real-estate, commercial or agricultural purposes, or municipal tap water. MyHealth Alberta advises testing for bacteria 2 times a year and for chemicals and trace metals every 3 years.
wells.cost: Free: AHS describes it as a free service (2015 AHS release); the current AHS and MyHealth Alberta pages describe the service without listing any fee.
wells.tests: Bacteria (total coliforms, E. coli); routine chemistry (pH, sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium, hardness, TDS, iron, alkalinity, chloride, fluoride, nitrite/nitrate, sulphate); trace metals (e.g., arsenic, lead, manganese).
wells.frequency: Bacteria 2 times a year; chemicals and trace metals every 3 years.
wells.bottles: AHS facilities/community health centres; see InformAlberta's 'Environmental Public Health - Water Sample Bottle Pick-up & Drop-off' listing.
wells.notes: AHS pick-up listings note the lab will not accept samples taken more than 24 hours before they arrive (e.g., Strathcona County Health Centre listing: https://www.albertahealthservices.ca/findhealth/Service.aspx?id=1083627&serviceAtFacilityID=1132297).

commercialRules.note: NRCan's list includes only Calgary's BenchmarkYYC and Edmonton's benchmarking program for Alberta, both voluntary per the cities' own pages.

evaluationPrices.note: No Alberta provincial evaluation rebate and no service-organization price list were found. Alberta CEIP municipalities require an EnerGuide evaluation but publish no price.

radon.buildingCode: Yes. Saskatchewan adopted the NBC 2020 (effective Jan 1, 2024) under The Construction Codes Act. NBC Sentence 9.13.4.2.(2) requires dwelling units to have a rough-in for subfloor depressurization (Article 9.13.4.3), plus an air-barrier soil-gas barrier.
radon.testKitProgram: Lung Saskatchewan sells long-term alpha-track kits for $65, including return shipping and lab analysis. It also supports free radon-monitor lending at eight libraries and library regions, including Regina Public Library and Saskatoon Public Library.
radon.other: The Saskatchewan Home Renovation Tax Credit was re-introduced for 2025 and later tax years (10.5% on up to $4,000 of eligible expenses, or $5,000 for seniors), and Lung Saskatchewan lists radon mitigation as eligible. Lung Saskatchewan says its Caring Breaths radon-mitigation assistance returns in 2026 (applications not yet open when checked).

radonNewer.figure: Approximately 1 in 3 at or above 200 Bq/m3 (unweighted value; no exact percentage given); geometric mean 140.7 Bq/m3 (unweighted).

coAlarms.appliesTo: All buildings with a residential occupancy that contain a fuel-burning appliance, an attached vehicle parking garage and/or multiple residential suites, regardless of construction date. From 2026-11-01, every residential suite.
coAlarms.summary: Saskatchewan's Building Code Regulations require CO alarms and smoke alarms (or combination units) in all residential buildings, regardless of when they were built. Enforcement began 2022-07-01. In homes, CO alarms go inside each sleeping room or within 5 m outside each sleeping-room door, plus in any room with a solid-fuel-burning appliance. 'Henry's Law', The Building Code (Henry Losco) Amendment Regulations, 2026, was introduced 2026-05-05 and comes into force 2026-11-01. It requires a CO alarm in every residential suite, including apartments, condos and houses with secondary suites, regardless of when the building was built or last renovated. It replaces the earlier practice of requiring alarms only in suites sharing a wall, floor or ceiling with a garage or service room.
coAlarms.law: The Construction Codes Act; The Building Code Regulations (retroactive CO/smoke alarm rule, enforced from 2022-07-01); The Building Code (Henry Losco) Amendment Regulations, 2026 (in force 2026-11-01)

asbestos.summary: Under The Saskatchewan Employment Act and The Occupational Health and Safety Regulations, 2020, building owners, contractors and employers must have a competent person inventory all asbestos-containing materials in a workplace building, inspect them regularly, and put safe work procedures and training in place. They must also notify Occupational Health and Safety at least 14 days before a high-risk asbestos process.
keyPoints: Any material likely to contain asbestos is treated as asbestos-containing until it is shown to be asbestos-free.

The Public Health Act, 1994 requires the provincial government, Crown corporations, health regions and public school facilities to provide and post asbestos information (Asbestos Registry of Public Buildings).
No homeowner-specific or landfill rule was checked for Saskatchewan.
asbestos.law: The Saskatchewan Employment Act; The Occupational Health and Safety Regulations, 2020; The Public Health Act, 1994 (public building registry)

wells.summary: Saskatchewan well owners can have their water tested for a fee at the Roy Romanow Provincial Laboratory (RRPL, Saskatchewan Health Authority), which distributes sample bottles to rural municipality (RM) offices and public health offices across the province. The SHA advises testing private supplies annually for total coliform bacteria and nitrate. RRPL's published fee schedule (effective April 1, 2017; the lab asks you to confirm current prices) lists $23 for total coliforms/E. coli, $29 for a 'water potability' panel (bacteria plus nitrate) and $104 for a general chemical analysis.
wells.cost: Fee-based (GST included, schedule effective April 1, 2017; confirm at 1-866-450-0000): total coliforms + E. coli $23.00; nitrate $11.50; water potability panel $29.00; general chemical/water quality analysis $104.00; arsenic $23.00.
wells.tests: Bacteriological (total coliforms, E. coli) and chemical tests (nitrate, fluoride, general chemistry panel; individual metals such as arsenic).
wells.frequency: Annually for total coliform bacteria and nitrate.
wells.bottles: RM offices and public health offices (supplied by RRPL), or from RRPL directly.

radon.buildingCode: Yes. The Manitoba Building Code (M.R. 78/2023, in force Jan 1, 2024) adopts the NBC 2020. Manitoba's amendments do not change Subsection 9.13.4 (Soil Gas Control), so the soil-gas barrier and the rough-in for subfloor depressurization apply.
radon.testKitProgram: No free provincial kit program found. The province's radon page points to the Manitoba Lung Association's kits and its Library Lending Program, and Take Action on Radon lists many Manitoba regional libraries that lend monitors free with a library card.
radon.other: Manitoba Hydro's Home Energy Efficiency Loan can finance radon mitigation up to $5,000 over 5 years (C-NRPP-certified contractor required). Lungs Matter mitigation aid (up to $1,500) is also available (Manitoba income cap $88,900).

coAlarms.appliesTo: Only buildings that must receive regular fire safety inspections under M.R. 208/2014, where a CO exposure risk exists: elderly persons' housing, personal care homes, home-type care occupancies, licensed child care centres, hospitals, schools, recreation centres, hotels/motels, licensed premises, and restaurants in buildings with dwelling units. Private houses are not on the list.
coAlarms.summary: The Manitoba Fire Code (M.R. 82/2023, in force 2024-01-01), Article 2.1.3.8, requires CO detection equipment only in buildings that must be inspected under the Fire Safety Inspections (2014) Regulation, where a CO exposure risk exists. Battery-operated alarms are allowed, and the equipment must be installed per the Manitoba Building Code. Ordinary private homes are not among the inspected building types, so there is no provincial retrofit requirement for them. The Manitoba Building Code's CO requirements for new homes were not verified.
coAlarms.law: Manitoba Fire Code, M.R. 82/2023, Div. B Art. 2.1.3.8; Fire Safety Inspections (2014) Regulation, M.R. 208/2014, s. 1

asbestos.summary: Part 37 of the Workplace Safety and Health Regulation applies to every workplace where asbestos is present. The employer and owner must keep an inventory of asbestos-containing material prepared by a qualified person, prevent asbestos release before alterations or renovations, remove releasable asbestos before demolition, and notify the branch 5 to 10 days before work that may release asbestos. M.R. 108/2025 (registered 2025-12-04) added WCB-approved training, asbestos certificates and a registry of asbestos businesses. From 2027-06-01, asbestos abatement and asbestos inventory (sampling) work will require a valid certificate, and employers will need to register.
keyPoints: Any material likely to contain asbestos is deemed asbestos-containing until a qualified person determines otherwise (s. 37.2(2)).

Provisions in force 2027-06-01: s. 37.10 (certificate required), s. 37.15(1) (registration), s. 37.19, s. 37.23(1)(a) (employers and owners may not permit uncertified asbestos work), plus related clauses.
No landfill rule was checked for Manitoba.
asbestos.law: Workplace Safety and Health Regulation, M.R. 217/2006, Part 37, as amended by M.R. 108/2025
asbestos.effective: Certification and registration requirements in force 2027-06-01

wells.summary: Manitoba subsidizes rather than provides free testing: its Private Well Testing Subsidy Program gives private well and cistern owners one subsidized bacteria test a year (total coliforms and E. coli) at Duracan Laboratory, 862 Dufferin Ave., Winnipeg, for $17.67 including tax, and a positive result comes with disinfection instructions and a coupon for a free re-test. The province says to test at least once a year, ideally in spring after snowmelt and after flooding or heavy rain. Bottles come from the lab, and some RM offices stock Duracan bottles.
wells.cost: $17.67 (tax included) for the once-a-year subsidized bacteria test; free re-test after a positive result. For flood-affected owners the subsidy was temporarily raised to 100% from June 15 to August 31, 2026. Chemical tests are not covered by the subsidy.
wells.tests: Subsidized test: total coliforms and E. coli.
wells.frequency: At least once a year (spring after snowmelt is ideal); also after flooding, heavy rain or changes in the water.
wells.bottles: From the lab (Duracan); some RM offices (e.g., RM of St. Clements) stock Duracan bottles; the 2019 provincial fact sheet also points to RM and Conservation District offices.
wells.notes: Manitoba publishes fact sheets on naturally occurring nitrate, arsenic, uranium, fluoride, manganese and other elements in well water, but we found no provincial chemistry-testing program.

Free evaluations through income-based and Indigenous offers. No service-organization price was found on Efficiency Manitoba's pages. Page modified June 4, 2026.

radon.buildingCode: Yes. The Nova Scotia Building Code Regulations (N.S. Reg. 198/2024) adopt the NBC 2020, effective Apr 1, 2025. They make no Nova Scotia amendment to Subsection 9.13.4, so the soil-gas barrier and the radon rough-in for subfloor depressurization apply.
radon.testKitProgram: LungNSPEI's Radon Reduction Grant Program, a pilot, provides free radon test kits to low-income Nova Scotia households and mitigation grants of up to $2,500. Its Radon Detector Library Loan Program has put 300+ short-term detectors in Nova Scotia and PEI public libraries. Both are listed on LungNSPEI's current site; no end date is given.
radon.other: Nova Scotia publishes an interactive Radon Risk Map (provincial map viewer). Lungs Matter mitigation aid (up to $1,500) is available to eligible households (NS income cap $79,900).

coAlarms.appliesTo: New construction under the Building Code: residential or care occupancy buildings with a fuel-burning appliance or storage garage. Existing buildings don't have to be retrofitted unless an official orders it.
coAlarms.summary: A Nova Scotia government CO document (December 2024) says the Building Code Regulations (which reference the National Building Code) require a CO alarm in a residential or care occupancy building that has a fuel-burning appliance or storage garage. It also says 'older buildings do not need to be retrofitted' when a new Code is adopted unless a Building Official or Fire Inspector requires more equipment because of unsafe conditions. The Fire Safety Regulations require CO alarms to be inspected, tested and maintained per the manufacturer's instructions. The same document says building owners 'should' install CO monitors in all buildings with fuel-burning equipment, which is a recommendation, not a requirement. Nova Scotia adopted the National Fire Code 2020 effective 2025-04-01.
coAlarms.law: Nova Scotia Building Code Regulations (new construction); Fire Safety Regulations, N.S. Reg. 48/2003 (maintenance)

asbestos.summary: The Asbestos Waste Management Regulations apply to any person, not just employers. Friable waste with more than 1% asbestos is 'waste dangerous goods'. Removal from a building must follow the Occupational Health and Safety Act codes of practice. The waste must be wetted, double-bagged in 6-mil bags (or bagged and put in a drum), shipped with a shipping document, and buried only at an approved site after the site has confirmed it will accept the waste.
keyPoints: Approved disposal: an active municipal solid-waste site approved to accept asbestos, an industrial site whose approval covers asbestos, or an approved waste disposal site (s. 19).
No homeowner pre-renovation survey requirement was found.
asbestos.law: Asbestos Waste Management Regulations, N.S. Reg. 53/95 (Environment Act), amended to N.S. Reg. 121/2017

wells.summary: More than 40% of Nova Scotia households get their drinking water from their own private wells. Owners pay for testing: bottles are picked up and samples dropped off at Nova Scotia Health (NSH) locations around the province (other labs also test drinking water), and NSH charges $34.50 for a total coliform/E. coli presence-absence test and $37.63 to $138.77 for its chemical packages. The province's current guidance is to test at least every year for bacteria and every five years for chemical contaminants, using a list of about 30 parameters that includes arsenic, uranium, lead, manganese, nitrate/nitrite and fluoride.
wells.cost: NSH fees: total coliform & E. coli presence/absence $34.50 (MPN count $46.00); chemical Package A (arsenic, uranium) $37.63, Package B $59.10, Package C $120.67, Package D $138.77.
wells.tests: Bacteria (total coliforms, E. coli); chemistry: province lists ~30 parameters (alkalinity, metals incl. arsenic, lead, manganese, uranium; nitrate/nitrite; fluoride; hardness; etc.).
wells.frequency: Bacteria at least every year; chemical contaminants every five years (surface-water supplies: bacteria every six months, chemistry yearly).
wells.bottles: NSH hospitals/health centres and some municipal offices (see the NSH water-testing pick-up/drop-off map).
wells.notes: NSH's water-testing page still cites an older recommendation (bacteria every six months, chemistry every two years); the novascotia.ca page is the current provincial guidance. Several eastern NSH sites currently redirect bacterial samples to Bureau Veritas in Sydney.

New Brunswick applies the NBC 2020 to construction, alteration and demolition under the Building Code Administration Act.

asbestos.summary: Under General Regulation 91-191 (OHS Act), Part III.1 (added 2022), owners of a place of employment, employers and contractors must adopt and follow WorkSafeNB's 'A Code of Practice for Working with Materials Containing Asbestos in New Brunswick' for employees who work with, near, or disturb asbestos-containing material. Employees must follow it too.
keyPoints: Regulation consolidated to 2026-06-30.

wells.summary: New Brunswick well owners pay for testing. RPC Analytical Services is the designated provincial analytical lab (offices in Fredericton and Moncton); water-testing kits with bottles and instructions are available at Service New Brunswick (SNB) offices or RPC, and samples go back to RPC, a designated SNB office or any ISO 17025-accredited lab. The province recommends testing for bacteria (total coliforms, E. coli) twice a year, ideally at spring thaw and during fall rains, and for inorganic contaminants (e.g., arsenic, uranium, fluoride, nitrate) when a well is drilled and every two years after.
wells.cost: Fee-based; prices are not published on the provincial or RPC pages (contact RPC).
wells.tests: Bacteria (total coliforms, E. coli); inorganics (e.g., arsenic, uranium, fluoride, nitrate); organics (petroleum, pesticides, solvents) where there is a specific risk.
wells.frequency: Bacteria twice a year (spring thaw, fall rains); inorganics at drilling and every two years after.
wells.bottles: Designated SNB offices or RPC Analytical Services (Fredericton, Moncton).
wells.notes: SNB offices accept samples only on certain days/mornings, so call ahead.

asbestos.summary: PEI's OHS General Regulations, Part 49, require that suspect material be treated as asbestos until a competent person shows otherwise, that only a competent person take samples, and that bulk samples go to a CALA- or AIHA-accredited lab. Workplaces with asbestos need an inventory (inspected yearly) and a management plan, all asbestos work must be done by a holder of an asbestos contractor's certificate (s. 49.9, valid 5 years), and releasable asbestos must be removed before demolition (s. 49.23).
keyPoints: Workers who handle, disturb or remove asbestos-containing material must complete an asbestos abatement course (s. 49.7(4)).
WCB PEI publishes an 'Asbestos Notification Permit' form.

Bottles and forms are available at the lab (23 Innovation Way, Charlottetown) or any Access PEI site, and samples can be dropped at Access PEI centres outside Charlottetown. The province recommends a bacteria test at least once a year and a chemical analysis when a well is first drilled and every 2 years after.

wells.tests: Bacteria (total coliforms, E. coli) and general chemistry.
wells.frequency: Bacteria at least once a year; chemistry when the well is drilled and every 2 years after.
wells.bottles: PEI Analytical Laboratories, 23 Innovation Way, Charlottetown, or any Access PEI site.

asbestos.summary: The Asbestos Abatement Regulations, 1998 cover workplaces and the repair, alteration or maintenance of a building containing asbestos, including its owner. Only holders of a valid asbestos abatement contractor's certificate may carry on the business of asbestos removal. The owner or contractor must notify the OHS Division in writing before starting and must obtain a disposal permit from the minister.

Chemical testing is not free and is done by private laboratories (the province keeps a list of approved labs). A provincial pilot launched in December 2022 handed out free chemistry test kits; we could not confirm whether it is still running.

Yukon enforces the NBC 2020 with territorial variations (enforced from Apr 1, 2023 per CBHCC); its Subsection 9.13.4 requires a soil-gas barrier and a radon rough-in for dwellings. Yukon plans to adopt the NBC 2025, which adds a passive radon stack, on June 22, 2027. Whether Yukon's territorial variations change 9.13.4 was not verified.
radon.testKitProgram: Yukon Public Libraries lend free radon screening kits from November 2025, available November to May (10 at Whitehorse Public Library plus one each in Dawson City, Haines Junction, Carmacks, Carcross and Watson Lake). Long-term kits must be bought separately.
radon.other: The Government of Yukon says there is radon in all Yukon communities and in every subdivision in Whitehorse.

coAlarms.appliesTo: Every Yukon residence with a fuel-burning appliance or an attached garage.
coAlarms.summary: The Yukon government states: 'Every Yukon residence with a fuel burning appliance or an attached garage must have CO detectors installed' (yukon.ca, modified 2026-01-02). The Oil-fired Appliance Safety Statutory Amendment Act (S.Y. 2013, c. 3) amended the Fire Prevention Act and Building Standards Act to allow regulations requiring owners or occupants to install and maintain CO detectors. A 2019-05-28 Yukon release says homes with gas-burning devices require CO and smoke detectors, and ties this to gas-fitting permits.
coAlarms.note: The implementing regulation's name and in-force date were not located (laws.yukon.ca blocks automated access).
coAlarms.law: Oil-fired Appliance Safety Statutory Amendment Act, S.Y. 2013, c. 3 (enabling amendments to the Fire Prevention Act and Building Standards Act); implementing regulation not verified

asbestos.summary: Before demolition or salvage of a building, a competent person must inspect and identify asbestos, lead and other hazardous materials, keep the results at the workplace, and have them contained or removed (OHS Regulations Part 10, s. 10.56). The Occupational Health Regulations' asbestos-control sections set restricted-area, waste-container, protective-equipment and medical-exam rules, and assign removal steps to an 'asbestos control contractor', defined as an employer certified by an accredited agency.
keyPoints: The asbestos control contractor must take bagged asbestos waste to a pre-arranged sanitary landfill site and make sure it is covered immediately.
s. 10.56 covers demolition and salvage; no Yukon renovation survey rule was found.
asbestos.law: Occupational Health Regulations (Asbestos Control, ss. 33+); Occupational Health and Safety Regulations Part 10, s. 10.56

wells.summary: Yukon's Environmental Health Services Water Laboratory (#2 Hospital Road, Whitehorse) tests well water for total coliforms and E. coli at no cost; owners get a sampling bottle and form by visiting the office or calling 867-667-8391 (toll-free 1-800-661-0408 ext. 8391), keep the sample cool and deliver it within 24 hours on the lab's receiving days. No Yukon lab tests drinking water for chemical, physical or radiological parameters, so those tests go to accredited labs in B.C. or Alberta at the owner's cost, often as much as $200 plus shipping for the 30 common parameters. The territory recommends bacteria testing at least once a year and chemistry for two consecutive years at first, then every five years if nothing changes.
wells.cost: Bacteria: free. Chemistry: paid to B.C./Alberta accredited labs, often as much as $200 plus shipping.
wells.tests: Free: total coliforms and E. coli. Chemistry (30 parameters incl. arsenic, uranium, lead, manganese, nitrate, fluoride) at out-of-territory labs.
wells.frequency: Bacteria at least once a year; chemistry 2 consecutive years initially, then every 5 years if no concerns.
wells.bottles: Environmental Health Services, #2 Hospital Road, Whitehorse (in person or by phone); chemistry labs supply their own bottles.

evaluationPrices.price: Existing homes: $50 for a pre-renovation assessment plus $50 for the return visit required for the insulation and air sealing rebate. New homes: $50 for a plan assessment and about $200 for the final assessment, blower door test and label.
evaluationPrices.note: Reduced-cost assessments arranged through the Yukon government's partnership with local energy advisors; the page does not state the subsidy amount. High demand, so appointments can take several weeks. Page modified 2024-12-02.

The Fire Prevention Regulations (amended by R-087-2024, in force 2024-10-01) adopt the National Building Code 2020 and National Fire Code 2020. Neither the Fire Prevention Act (latest amendments in force 2026-07-02) nor the Regulations contain a CO alarm provision.
coAlarms.note: No official NWT statement was found that explicitly confirms or rules out a CO alarm requirement for existing homes. Left null.
coAlarms.law: Fire Prevention Act (RSNWT 1988, c. F-6); Fire Prevention Regulations (RRNWT 1990, c. F-12), as amended by R-087-2024

asbestos.summary: WSCC's Asbestos Abatement Code of Practice (NWT and Nunavut, in effect 2018-09-28, adapted from Alberta's manual) gives the practical requirements for workplaces under the Safety Act and OHS Regulations. It calls a building survey an important step before renovating or demolishing pre-1980 buildings, and says waste asbestos is a contaminant under the NWT Environmental Protection Act that must be managed as hazardous waste, in sealed, impervious containers.
keyPoints: The GNWT 'Guideline for the Management of Waste Asbestos' (2004), quoted in the Code, defines asbestos waste as material with more than 1% asbestos by weight.
asbestos.law: Safety Act and Occupational Health and Safety Regulations (NWT); WSCC Asbestos Abatement Code of Practice (2018)

Private citizens can use the GNWT's Taiga Environmental Laboratory in Yellowknife (Department of Environment and Climate Change), which supplies sampling bottles free (shipping extra). Its July 2021 price guide lists total coliforms + E. coli (drinking water) at $28 per sample and an annual drinking-water chemistry package at $380 per sample, with prices subject to change.
wells.cost: Fee-based at Taiga (2021 price guide: $28 bacteria; $380 annual drinking-water chemistry package); no free program found.
wells.tests: Bacteria (total coliforms, E. coli); chemistry packages (metals incl. arsenic, uranium, lead; nitrate; fluoride; etc.).
wells.bottles: Taiga Environmental Laboratory provides sampling supplies free of charge (pick-up in Yellowknife or shipped).
wells.notes: Frequency is null: no NWT recommendation for private wells was found. NCCEH (2013) notes that larger NWT communities have piped and/or trucked water systems, while many smaller settlements have no central water supply.

evaluationPrices.note: Subsidized EnerGuide evaluations of existing homes, in effect since May 1, 2025 (up from $150). AEA also gives free advice. New-home evaluations are fee-based per the application form; the City of Yellowknife requires EnerGuide evaluations for new homes started after June 25, 2018.

radon.guideline: Health Canada's radon guideline is 200 Bq/m3, the annual average in the normal occupancy area (anywhere a person spends more than 4 hours a day). Above that, Health Canada recommends corrective action within 1 year, sooner for higher levels, and keeping exposure as low as reasonably achievable (ALARA).
radon.testLength: Health Canada says to do a long-term test for a minimum of 3 months. Its measurement guide says at least 91 days of the test should fall in the heating season, because heating-season tests give a conservative (higher) estimate. Test in a normal occupancy area on the lowest lived-in level. Provincial pages phrase this as at least 3 months, ideally in winter (e.g. October to April).
radon.cnrpp: C-NRPP's "Find a Professional" page (c-nrpp.ca/find-a-professional/) embeds a search tool (app.c-nrpp.ca/findaprofessional). You can search by postal code (with distance), by province or by service area, and filter by certification: Residential or Commercial Measurement, Residential or Commercial Mitigation, and CRNCH (Controlling Radon in New Canadian Homes). So it lists both measurement and mitigation professionals by location. Provincial pages (e.g. New Brunswick, Québec) direct homeowners to it.

radonSurvey.title: Cross-Canada Survey of Radon Concentrations in Homes - Final Report
radonSurvey.note: Figures are from Table 5, the raw percentages by health region (2007 health-region boundaries), based on long-term tests during the 2009-10 and 2010-11 fall/winter seasons (about 14,000 homes). The table was read on the canada.ca page and verified line by line against the PDF edition (https://publications.gc.ca/collections/collection_2012/sc-hc/H144-2-2012-eng.pdf). pct200to600 is an extra field taken from the same table.

vermiculite.summary: Health Canada says vermiculite-based insulation may contain asbestos. If it is in your attic or walls: don't use the attic for storage, keep children out, and don't disturb it or try to remove it yourself. Seal gaps around the attic hatch, baseboards, light fixtures, electrical outlets and window/door frames, and repair cracks or holes in walls and ceilings. If you plan to renovate, hire professionals trained to handle asbestos. (Page modified 2023-02-10.)

provincialNotes.QC: Québec.ca says some vermiculite insulation sold between 1920 and 1990 may contain asbestos. It advises limiting attic access, leaving removal and attic renovation to a qualified professional, never trying to remove it yourself, and sealing and caulking openings. https://www.quebec.ca/sante/conseils-et-prevention/sante-et-environnement/prevenir-les-effets-amiante-sur-la-sante
provincialNotes.AB: For workplaces, the Alberta Asbestos Abatement Manual says vermiculite often contains asbestos below 1% but can still release hazardous fibre levels when disturbed. Without data showing it is uncontaminated, it is assumed contaminated, and known or suspected contaminated vermiculite must be treated as asbestos-containing material. https://www.alberta.ca/alberta-asbestos-abatement-manual

leadPaint.summary: Health Canada (page modified 2025-09-09) says a home built before 1960 probably contains lead-based paint. If it was built between 1960 and 1990, the exterior paint may contain lead, and its 'Reduce your exposure to lead' page adds that interior paint may contain smaller but still harmful amounts. Homes built after 1990 should not contain lead paint, because consumer paints in Canada and the U.S. were virtually lead-free by then. To test, send paint chip samples to a lab or hire a contractor with the proper X-ray equipment. Do not use sanders, heat guns or blowlamps to remove it; keep children and pregnant women away from the work area.
leadPaint.provincialNotes: No provincial lead-paint rule aimed at homeowners was found. Workplace rules touch it indirectly: B.C. OHS Regulation s. 20.112 includes lead in the hazardous-materials inspection required before demolition or renovation, and Yukon OHS Regulations s. 10.56 includes lead in the pre-demolition inspection.

mould.summary: Health Canada's Residential Indoor Air Quality Guideline: Moulds (2007) sets no numerical exposure limit. It recommends controlling humidity, promptly repairing water damage, and thoroughly cleaning any visible or concealed mould. Health Canada's consumer page (modified 2023-02-13) says there is no 'safe' limit and recommends 30–50% relative humidity. It classifies mould as small (1–3 patches, each under 1 m²), medium (more than 3 patches, or patches between 1 and 3 m²) or extensive (over 3 m², where you should consider a professional), and says testing mould concentrations or species is usually unnecessary.
mould.provincialNotes: No province was found with a mandatory residential mould standard; this was not exhaustively checked for every province (for example, tenancy and property-standards rules). Quebec has a voluntary standard, BNQ 3009-600 'Contamination des habitations par les moisissures — Investigation et réhabilitation du bâtiment', published 2020-04-28. It applies to houses and multi-unit dwellings, new or old, owner-occupied or rented, and the BNQ describes it as a 'document d'application volontaire'. https://www.quebec.ca/nouvelles/actualites/details/bnq-3009-600-la-premiere-norme-quebecoise-sur-les-moisissures-dans-les-habitations

labs.asbestos: Bulk building-material samples are analysed by polarized light microscopy (PLM). Options: (1) NVLAP (U.S. NIST) Asbestos Fiber Analysis program, which covers bulk PLM (NIST Handbook 150-3) and airborne TEM, with a searchable directory of accredited labs. (2) AIHA-LAP's Industrial Hygiene program (IHLAP), which accredits PLM, PCM and TEM methods, searchable in the AIHA-LAP directory. (3) The Standards Council of Canada's accredited-organizations search (ISO/IEC 17025 labs, filterable by province and field). (4) The CALA Directory of Accredited Laboratories (ISO/IEC 17025 environmental labs, searchable by parameter and method). In Quebec, the IRSST 'CQ Vrac' program lists labs recognized for asbestos in bulk materials (IRSST method 244 PLM; TEM for non-friable materials), and Quebec's regulatory threshold is 0.1%, versus 0.5% in Ontario, so reports must be able to show that level. PEI's OHS rules require bulk asbestos samples to go to a CALA- or AIHA-accredited lab.
labs.mould: AIHA-LAP's Environmental Microbiology program (EMLAP) accredits labs for fungal direct examination (e.g., spore-trap air samples, tape lifts) and culturable analysis. Search the AIHA-LAP directory and filter by EMLAP. Health Canada notes that measuring mould concentrations or identifying species is usually not needed.
labs.lead: AIHA-LAP's Environmental Lead program (ELLAP) accredits labs for lead in paint, soil, settled dust and air. All ELLAP labs are also recognized under the U.S. EPA National Lead Laboratory Accreditation Program. Health Canada says you can send paint chips to a lab or hire a contractor with X-ray equipment. The SCC and CALA directories list ISO/IEC 17025 labs; check each lab's scope for lead in paint.

commercialFederal.name: ENERGY STAR Portfolio Manager (administered in Canada by NRCan)
commercialFederal.summary: Free online benchmarking platform 'administered and promoted by Natural Resources Canada'; tracks energy (plus water and waste) and gives a 1-100 ENERGY STAR score (75+ can apply for certification). NRCan says it can be used for provincial, territorial and municipal reporting programs; it is the submission tool named by Ontario EWRB, Toronto, Vancouver, Victoria, Saanich and Montréal. NRCan also supports utilities' automated data exchange (Portfolio Manager Web Services).
commercialFederal.note: No federal mandatory benchmarking/reporting rule for private buildings was found; NRCan's own jurisdiction list (modified 2026-03-26) names only provincial and municipal programs.

commercialFederal.name: NRCan list of Canadian benchmarking / building performance standard programs
commercialFederal.summary: Under 'Benchmarking and disclosure (regulation or voluntary program)' NRCan lists Ontario EWRB, Montréal's GHG disclosure and rating by-law, Calgary BenchmarkYYC, Edmonton's Building Energy Benchmarking Program, Ottawa's benchmarking and auditing program, Winnipeg's Building Energy Disclosure Project, Efficiency Nova Scotia's Benchmarking Pilot, a Service New Brunswick energy management annual report, two Quebec items, Building Benchmark BC and the CaGBC Disclosure Challenge. Under 'Building performance standards' it lists Vancouver (carbon pollution limits and reporting) and Toronto (Energy & Water Reporting).
commercialFederal.note: Not exhaustive or fully current: it omits Victoria's and Saanich's 2025 reporting bylaws and Quebec's June 2026 provincial regulation, and it doesn't separate mandatory from voluntary programs.

enbridge-commercial-audits.name: Commercial Custom Audits & Studies - Energy Assessments and Meters
enbridge-commercial-audits.summary: Pays up to 50% of eligible costs for energy audits, engineering feasibility studies, steam trap surveys/audits, air and water balancing and metering. The cap depends on the address's previous-year gas use: up to $6,000 (100,000 to under 3,000,000 m3), up to $10,000 (3,000,000 to under 10,000,000 m3), up to $20,000 (10,000,000 m3+, institutions only). Institutions max $20,000 per project; other commercial sectors max $10,000 per project.
enbridge-commercial-audits.eligibility: Enbridge Gas Inc. customers using at least 100,000 m3 of natural gas in the previous year at that address; pre-approval required; one opportunity-identification incentive per address; applicants and Business Partners limited to 5 such projects per year not linked to a completed Custom Retrofit project.

enbridge-affordable-housing-assessment.name: Affordable Housing Multi-Residential Program - energy assessment
enbridge-affordable-housing-assessment.summary: Up to $8,000 for an energy assessment (up to $40,000 per housing provider) to find natural gas savings in affordable housing buildings.
enbridge-affordable-housing-assessment.eligibility: Affordable housing providers (Enbridge Gas customers); detailed criteria are on the program page (not read in this pass).
enbridge-affordable-housing-assessment.note: Multi-residential affordable housing only - not general commercial.

saveonenergy-small-business.name: Save on Energy Small Business Program
saveonenergy-small-business.summary: Free on-site assessment by qualified Save on Energy representatives, then free installed upgrades: up to $3,000 for lighting and up to $2,500 for refrigeration and smart thermostats (up to $5,500 total).
saveonenergy-small-business.eligibility: Ontario businesses with 50 or fewer employees that own or lease their space (tenants need landlord consent).
saveonenergy-small-business.note: No end date shown; no closure notice in Save on Energy news (checked 2026-09-28).

saveonenergy-ebcx.name: Existing Building Commissioning (EBCx) Program
saveonenergy-ebcx.summary: Funds retro-commissioning. Investigation phase: up to $0.06 per sq ft, max $50,000 per application or 75% of the participant's cost for the commissioning provider. Implementation and persistence phases: $0.03 per kWh of confirmed/persisting savings (each capped at 30% of annual consumption or $50,000, whichever is lower).
saveonenergy-ebcx.eligibility: Buildings with 12+ months of consecutive energy data, using at least 750,000 kWh/yr (excluding industrial process loads), no commissioning in the last two years, connected to the IESO-controlled grid (directly or behind the meter).

saveonenergy-xlerate.name: XLerate Program - Project Feasibility Study funding
saveonenergy-xlerate.summary: Project feasibility study (PFS) funding at a 50% cost share; project incentives of $300/MWh up to 75% of eligible costs (max $15 million per project).
saveonenergy-xlerate.eligibility: Industrial, municipal, institutional and healthcare sectors; projects must save at least 600 MWh of electricity per year. Not aimed at commercial office/retail.

saveonenergy-bizenergysaver.name: BizEnergySaver Program (local initiative)
saveonenergy-bizenergysaver.summary: Free on-site assessment plus direct installation, with instant discounts applied on the invoice (most VFD upgrades now free).
saveonenergy-bizenergysaver.eligibility: Non-residential customers of Toronto Hydro, Hydro Ottawa or Hydro One with industrial, commercial, institutional or multi-unit residential facilities in eligible areas: all Toronto 'M' postal codes (expanded to all of Toronto on July 23, 2026) and Ottawa FSAs K1A, K1B, K1C, K1E, K1G, K1H, K1J, K1K, K1L, K1M, K1N, K1P, K1R, K1S, K1T, K1V, K1W, K1X, K1Y, K1Z, K2A, K2B, K2C, K2E, K2G, K2H, K2J, K2K, K2L, K2M, K2P, K2R, K2S, K2T, K2V, K2W, K4A, K4B, K4M, K4P.
saveonenergy-bizenergysaver.note: Installations must be completed by Aug 31, 2027.

toronto-building-tune-up.name: Building Tune-Up Program
toronto-building-tune-up.provider: City of Toronto (delivered by Enerva Energy Solutions)
toronto-building-tune-up.summary: Free expert on-site building assessment (the City says these typically cost $5,000 or more), a customized report of energy-performance opportunities, implementation support, staff training and a follow-up meeting.
toronto-building-tune-up.eligibility: Non-profits, community organizations, faith groups and small businesses (up to 50 employees); buildings generally 10,000-30,000 sq ft; condominiums and buildings 50,000 sq ft+ excluded. Participation is limited.

kitchener-utilities-cii.name: Commercial, industrial and institutional customer rebate programs
kitchener-utilities-cii.provider: Kitchener Utilities (City of Kitchener gas utility)
kitchener-utilities-cii.summary: Kitchener Utilities says CII customers planning equipment upgrades that save natural gas or cut carbon should email it for current rebate programs. It publishes no amounts and no audit/study incentive.
kitchener-utilities-cii.eligibility: Kitchener Utilities commercial, industrial and institutional gas customers.
kitchener-utilities-cii.note: Whether audits or studies are funded is not stated; contact utilities@kitchener.ca.

hydroquebec-energy-analysis.name: Efficient Solutions Program - Energy Analysis component
hydroquebec-energy-analysis.summary: Pays for eligible costs of an energy analysis (including in-house labour): 40% of eligible costs when the report is accepted and 60% after at least one measure is implemented (up to 100% in total). Caps for energy-efficiency analyses: existing buildings with 1-2 GWh reference use, $8,000 + $12,000 ($20,000 total), analysis must identify at least 100,000 kWh/yr of savings; over 2 GWh, $20,000 + $30,000 ($50,000 total), at least 200,000 kWh/yr. Analyses that also cover demand-response measures: up to $60,000 ($24,000 + $36,000 for buildings over 2 GWh).
hydroquebec-energy-analysis.eligibility: Commercial, institutional or industrial buildings in Quebec using at least 1 GWh/yr, supplied by the Hydro-Québec grid or an eligible off-grid, municipal or co-op system (including Hydro-Sherbrooke and Hydro-Jonquière/Ville de Saguenay). Submit a proposal and get approval before starting.

energir-feasibility-study.name: Energy audit and implementation - Feasibility Study grant
energir-feasibility-study.summary: 50% of the pre-tax cost of a feasibility study, max $50,000. Follow-on implementation grant: $1 per m3 of natural gas saved in the first year (max $1,000,000 per account), plus up to $15,000 for energy tracking.
energir-feasibility-study.eligibility: Current or future Énergir customers in commercial, multi-residential (4+ units), institutional or industrial sectors whose building is mainly heated with natural gas; the study must be done by a registered consulting engineering firm (OIQ engineer) and submitted to Énergir before the study starts.
energir-feasibility-study.note: Current participant guide applies to applications from Nov 1, 2023.

energir-recommissioning.name: Recommissioning of mechanical systems grant
energir-recommissioning.summary: Investigation phase: 75% of eligible costs; implementation: $1 per m3 of gas saved up to 75% of eligible costs (measures with payback over 1 year); transfer and continuous-monitoring phases: 75% of eligible costs. Up to $100,000 per project in total.
energir-recommissioning.eligibility: Énergir customers; buildings or building groups using at least 75,000 m3 of gas per year (smaller with Énergir approval); must use an accredited RCx agent (MELCCFP list); no Recommissioning or New Construction payment in the last five years.

enbridge-gaz-quebec-feasibility.name: Feasibility study financial assistance
enbridge-gaz-quebec-feasibility.summary: Up to $2,500 toward a feasibility study or an energy simulation (e.g., EE4, CAN-QUEST, DOE2); follow-on custom project incentive of $1 per m3 of gas saved.
enbridge-gaz-quebec-feasibility.eligibility: Enbridge Gaz Québec business customers (it serves the City of Gatineau and the Municipality of Chelsea).

qc-ecoperformance-analysis.name: ÉcoPerformance - Analyse de mesures de réduction des GES
qc-ecoperformance-analysis.summary: Standard analysis (energy study, fuel-switching study, fugitive-emissions study): 50% of eligible expenses, max $25,000 per site for small/medium energy users (under 36,000 GJ/yr non-electric) or $75,000 for large users. Complex analysis: 75%, max $100,000 / $300,000. Paid 50% on the signed purchase order and the rest after the engineer-signed report is accepted; project must finish within 24 months.
qc-ecoperformance-analysis.eligibility: Businesses, institutions, municipalities and organizations in industrial, commercial, agricultural, agri-food, manufacturing, institutional or municipal sectors with a Quebec site that burns fossil fuels (or has fugitive/process emissions). The report must be signed by an OIQ engineer.
qc-ecoperformance-analysis.note: New program framework in force July 7, 2026. Electric-only buildings (no fossil fuel use) are not eligible.

qc-ecoperformance-rcx.name: ÉcoPerformance - Remise au point des systèmes mécaniques (RCx)
qc-ecoperformance-rcx.summary: Former recommissioning funding component of ÉcoPerformance.
qc-ecoperformance-rcx.note: No new applications since Sept 1, 2026; component removed from the program framework. Énergir's recommissioning grant is still open.

bchydro-integrated-energy-audit.name: Integrated energy audit
bchydro-integrated-energy-audit.summary: Up to 100% funding for an energy expert (Alliance of Energy Professionals member) to audit a whole facility or selected systems; payment usually goes directly to the energy expert.
bchydro-integrated-energy-audit.eligibility: Industrial and large commercial customers; large commercial customers need company-wide electricity use of at least 2 GWh/yr. Applications go through a BC Hydro Key Account Manager or Regional Energy Manager.

bchydro-feasibility-study.name: Feasibility study
bchydro-feasibility-study.summary: Study 100% funded when the opportunity exceeds 200,000 kWh/yr or 100 kW; 50% funded for 25,000-200,000 kWh/yr or 25-100 kW (efficiency, efficient electrification or demand response).
bchydro-feasibility-study.eligibility: Industrial and large commercial customers (large commercial: company-wide use of at least 2 GWh/yr); energy expert must be an Alliance of Energy Professionals member; arranged through a Key Account Manager or Regional Energy Manager.

bc-continuous-optimization.name: Continuous Optimization (C-Op) program
bc-continuous-optimization.provider: BC Hydro in partnership with FortisBC
bc-continuous-optimization.summary: Funding of up to $0.15 per sq ft for an approved service provider to retro-commission or recommission HVAC and other systems; 75% is paid after the investigation stage and 25% on completion.
bc-continuous-optimization.eligibility: Owners or long-term leaseholders of existing large commercial or institutional buildings of 40,000 sq ft+ with a DDC building automation system with remote access; must work with a BC Hydro Key Account Manager/Regional Energy Manager (or, in FortisBC's electric territory, a FortisBC technical advisor). FortisBC adds: commercial-rate gas and/or FortisBC electric customer, no recommissioning in the last 5 years, 1+ year of FortisBC billing history.

fortisbc-commercial-energy-assessment.name: Commercial Energy Assessment Program
fortisbc-commercial-energy-assessment.summary: Free walkthrough energy assessment by a FortisBC-authorized consultant, with a report within 60 days listing low/no-cost measures, possible upgrades and applicable FortisBC rebates.
fortisbc-commercial-energy-assessment.eligibility: FortisBC commercial gas and/or electricity customers (or municipal electric customers of Grand Forks, Penticton, Summerland or Nelson Hydro); owner, long-term leaseholder or property manager; building occupied by the participant for at least 1 year; non-residential rate class.
